title: Care reform begins, housing supply shrinks, electricity bills
summary:
Spain's disability and dependency reforms take effect, while fewer homes are available for sale nationwide. We cover electricity prices, voting challenges, planned protests and tax developments, plus the latest on shamonda virus monitoring.

Enjoying Spain Daily? Support us: https://buymeacoffee.com/spanified

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Getting care recognised should mean less waiting from today—

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: —with Spain's new dependency rules? right Hold on. How much less?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The maximum wait is being halved. That's quite a change.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Especially when waiting means waiting for support you actually need.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Good morning! It's Friday, the twenty-third of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: I'm Dima, here with Inna. Today, electricity contract renewals and a challenge over voting rights. First, Spain's care reform.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Spain's disability and dependency reforms take effect today, Europa Press reports. The maximum recognition wait falls to three months. Benefits and services can be combined, and telecare becomes a right. The state must fund half the dependency system. Neighbours and friends can become officially recognised carers, and dependency assessments can lead to automatic disability recognition.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Wait, friends can be recognised too? Inna, that brings the rules closer to how people actually help each other.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It does. Support doesn't always come from a relative. exactly And combining services means fewer forced choices.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: But does that reach beyond arranging care? What about making someone's building accessible?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The reform requires homeowners' communities to apply for accessibility grants, Dima. It also bans higher insurance prices for disabled people.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So you have changes inside the home and outside it. mhm The paperwork touches quite a lot of daily life.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's why the recognition process matters so much. It's the route to support, not just another certificate.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: On health monitoring, 20 Minutos reports Spain's Agriculture Ministry is following shamonda virus after a death reported in France. The infected person was severely immunocompromised. French authorities have identified no health risk to the general population and are investigating. Spain has confirmed cattle outbreaks in six provinces since September, and the ministry calls for calm.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The ministry says it is in permanent contact with France, the regions and health authorities.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: In cattle, it spreads by mosquito bites. It doesn't kill the animal, but it affects milk production.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For homebuyers, the choice of properties has narrowed nationally. Expansión reports Idealista's finding that listings fell nine percent year on year in the third quarter. Valencia bucked that trend with a fifteen percent increase, while Madrid also gained stock. Idealista says high prices are pushing buyers away from big-city markets, reducing pressure on available homes.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Huh. More listings in those cities doesn't necessarily mean more people can afford to buy.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's Idealista's explanation: some buyers are being priced out. true More choice can sit alongside a difficult budget.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: A longer shortlist isn't much comfort if every flat is beyond your budget.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Household bills offer a different comparison. La Vanguardia reports Spanish electricity averaged about twenty-five cents per kilowatt-hour in the year's first half. The EU average was about twenty-eight cents, with renewables helping Spain. Iberdrola chairman Ignacio Galán warned on October twenty-first that prices would keep rising, reaching free-market customers as annual contracts renew.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Oof. So the renewal date is where that warning becomes relevant to someone's household budget.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Exactly. sure Being below the European average doesn't help much if you're on a free-market contract that's about to renew.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Staying with energy, El País reports that the National Court has temporarily suspended payments of the energy levy by energy company Repsol. The disputed assessments total more than two hundred and seventy million euros. Repsol's appeal continues, with the levy still being contested in court.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's a lot to leave pending. Why did the court agree to pause it?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For the 2023 assessment, the judge said immediate payment would risk the purpose of the appeal. For 2024, there was no opposition to the interim measure.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Three citizens naturalised under the Ley de Nietos, the law for descendants of Spanish exiles, have appealed to the Supreme Court. 20 Minutos reports a court order suspends their vote on November twenty-ninth. The main case concerns a Justice Ministry instruction presuming exile status for people who fled Spain between 1936 and 1955. Those with a consular certificate proving qualifying family exile are exempt.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hold on. For affected citizens abroad, that consular certificate could be central to whether they can cast a ballot.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: It could. The appeal argues that the suspension violates voting rights and equality, while the main case remains open.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Staying with the election, Europa Press reports agreement on a head-to-head debate on November sixteenth, on a private channel, between Socialist prime ministerial candidate Pedro Sánchez and opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo. A separate four-way debate with Vox and Frente Amplio remains disputed. The Socialists want public broadcaster TVE, while the People's Party proposes the private broadcaster Atresmedia.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: And the election itself is when again?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The twenty-ninth of November. So the debates would come in the last stretch of the campaign.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On industrial action, employers' organisation CEOE won't challenge the November eleventh general strike before it happens. Sources told the news agency EFE yesterday, Heraldo reports. CEOE president Antonio Garamendi had previously said he would contest it. Unions called the strike over housing and wages, saying mass afternoon demonstrations will be central to its success.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So the unions are putting particular weight on participation after the working day, rather than workplace stoppages alone.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: They are. Workers and people relying on transport have a nationwide strike date to keep in mind.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Farmers also plan a tractor protest in Madrid on October twenty-eighth over high costs and low prices. Expansión reports a draft farm tax order for next year would cut the net yield under the income tax modules system by ten percent. It includes diesel and fertiliser incentives. Farm groups call the twenty-cent-per-litre agricultural diesel discount wholly insufficient.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The proposed tax relief hasn't persuaded farm groups to call off their protest, then.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: No. The draft is open for consultation, while the tractor protest remains planned and could disrupt travel in the capital.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On a more serious note, El Diario reports a Nature study attributing over five thousand Spanish deaths to climate-driven extreme heat this summer. Across the European cities studied, it estimates fifty thousand heat-related deaths. Barcelona had Europe's second-highest death toll. Madrid had the highest share of deaths attributed to high temperatures.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The findings put a human cost behind the summer temperatures, especially in those large cities.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: They do. The study examines deaths linked to heat, including the additional toll attributed to human-caused warming.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For people handling an inheritance, Expansión reports a Supreme Court ruling on when income must be declared. Heirs must include estate income in personal income tax from the date of death. That applies even when the will delays accepting or using assets for years. The court rejected the argument that this duplicates Inheritance Tax.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Wait, income tax can begin before the heir is allowed to enjoy the assets?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's the consequence for wills with those delayed-use conditions. The tax timetable doesn't wait for access to the assets.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: On business taxation, El País reports Spain's multinational minimum tax collected about forty-six million euros through August, far below initial forecasts. It applies to groups with revenue above seven hundred and fifty million euros. This year's payments use results from two years ago, following a scaling back of the international tax project.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Oh. Is that because the international deal lost steam?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Partly, yes. The OECD negotiations stalled, so Spain's public finances get far less than forecast.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Madrid's Assembly approved its Taxpayer Defence Law yesterday, Expansión reports, with People's Party and Vox support and left-wing opposition. For taxes the state has ceded to the region, it sets a three-month reply deadline. A new complaints office gets fifteen working days to respond. The law takes effect the day after publication in the regional gazette.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A deadline for the administration too. Does that cover inheritance and property transfer taxes?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Those are included. oh nice Complaints can concern delays, electronic problems or mistreatment, giving taxpayers a specific route to raise them.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For people seeking debt relief, Expansión reports an EU court legal adviser's opinion supporting Spanish restrictions. A final tax-liability decision within the previous ten years can block cancellation unless the debt was paid in full. The case involves a man liable for more than forty thousand euros in company taxes. The opinion isn't a final ruling.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Mm. So someone seeking a fresh start can still face a barrier because of company tax liability?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's the issue in this case. The Spanish restriction looks at that final liability decision and whether payment was completed.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And a measure aimed at easing fuel shortages: 20 Minutos reports a December fifteenth deadline for releasing reserves. Spanish operators and distributors must release four point four million barrels of diesel and kerosene. The requirement implements Spain's reserve-release plan following the March agreement among International Energy Agency members.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Why is Spain doing it?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Because of supply shortages linked to the Middle East crisis, which are affecting fuel markets and prices.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Today's takeaway: wider care rights begin, with the recognition process central to getting people the support they need.
